blocks.text: Barkpark · Cloud · shared-tier doctrine
Shared Cells — shared hosting without the sins

content.value: Shared hosting has the worst reputation in infrastructure — earned over twenty years of LAMP boxes where one tenant's bad day became everyone's. Barkpark's shared tier only deserves to exist if we can name

, show which ones this architecture structurally cannot commit, and write doctrine for the rest. This paper is that ledger, and the synthesis: cells, not silos — with a graduation path instead of a ceiling.
Shared hosting earned its bad name from a sin Barkpark cannot commit: executing strangers' code on the same box.

blocks.text: Why shared hosting got its bad name

content.value: — PHP with filesystem access — on a cooperative-scheduled stack. Every sin follows from that: one infinite loop starved the box (no preemption), one compromised WordPress owned every neighbor (shared filesystem, shared user contexts), inode limits hid until you hit them, and accounts were so sticky that rebalancing meant a support ticket and a weekend. A Barkpark shared cell is a different animal: tenants author

, not code. The workload is structured writes and cacheable reads against one well-understood schema. That single fact deletes the worst caveat outright — but not all of them. Here is the honest ledger.

blocks.text: The caveat ledger — all ten, honestly

rows.value: 1 · Noisy neighbor
One PHP loop starves the box; no preemption.
Weaker by construction: BEAM preempts by reductions — no tenant can hog a scheduler. Real risks are shared Postgres connections, disk, and vips media work.
Per-workspace rate limits + PG connection budget + media queue with backpressure; pressure score per workspace; hot tenant → graduate, don't throttle-to-death.
2 · Security blast radius
Tenant code execution → one hacked plugin owns the box.
No tenant code runs, ever.
bp sites
is static-only. Residual risk is app bugs: scoping leaks, SSRF via webhooks, media-parser CVEs.
Defense in depth: app scoping + Postgres RLS as second wall; egress-filtered webhooks; vips in a sandboxed queue worker; shared-cell profile fences every instance-admin surface (tmux console OFF).
3 · Data isolation
Shared MySQL, tenant-visible filesystems.
One Postgres, workspace_id row scoping;
multi_tenant?/0
fail-closed. A scoping bug is still a cross-tenant leak.
Add RLS policies keyed on a per-request
app.workspace_id
GUC — the same bug must now be made twice, in two layers, to leak.
4 · Fate sharing
Box dies → hundreds down for hours; restore = ticket.
Same physics — a cell outage hits every tenant on it.
Cap cell size (~100 workspaces); blue/green per cell; archive/resurrect drills; per-workspace restore so one tenant's recovery never waits on the cell's.
5 · IP & mail reputation
One spammer blacklists the shared IP for everyone.
Identical risk if cells send mail directly.
Shared cells never send directly — all mail through the central DKIM relay with per-tenant signing + outbound rate caps; abuse freezes the workspace, not the cell.
6 · Performance ceiling
Hit the wall → buy a VPS → migrate by hand over a weekend.
The cell is still finite.
The ceiling becomes a door: live workspace migration to a dedicated box, domain intact (domains-table cutover). Graduation is an upsell moment, not an outage.
7 · Backup granularity
Account backups existed — restores were slow, lossy, ticket-driven.
Instance-level archive/resurrect exists; per-workspace does not yet.
Per-workspace export/bundle — the keystone primitive (see below). Self-serve restore from Studio.
8 · Upgrade coupling
PHP upgrade breaks half the tenants at once.
One BEAM per cell → all tenants upgrade together; a regression hits the whole cell.
Canary cells first (the fleet already deploys blue/green); version pinning is a dedicated-tier feature, stated honestly, not promised on shared.
9 · Compliance & residency
“Where is my data?” — no answer.
A cell lives in exactly one region; per-tenant residency inside a shared cell is impossible.
Region-pinned cells (EU default, Hetzner); residency choosers pick their cell at signup; strict-compliance customers are pointed at dedicated — honestly, at signup, not after.
10 · Hidden limits
Inode caps and CPU-seconds discovered only at the wall; silent failure.
Nothing hidden yet because no limits exist yet — the gap cuts both ways.
Quotas are a visible product surface: live meters in Studio +
bp usage
, soft limits with grace windows, never a silent write failure. Transparency IS the differentiator.

items.label: tenancy
items.text: docs/contracts/tenancy.md: multi_tenant?/0 rescues to true; create_workspace_with_owner/2 atomic; delete_workspace/1 is the only safe teardown and already walks media + documents + lifecycle hooks — the suspend/evict path inherits this.

items.label: tmux
items.lead: The console is ON by default, admin-gated.
items.text: Studio ships a browser terminal into host tmux, opt-out via BARKPARK_TMUX_CONSOLE=0. Fine on a single-tenant box; on a shared cell it must be hard-off in the boot profile — a host shell within reach of a scoping bug is not a risk shared hosting gets to take.

items.label: two layers
items.text: The error-emitter duplication lesson: contract-shape fixes had to be made in query_controller AND legacy_controller. Scoping code has forks too; RLS makes the database the layer that doesn't fork.

items.label: mail
items.lead: The relay is built and DKIM-verified.
items.text: Self-hosted Postfix+DKIM sidecar is done and verified against queued bytes — central per-tenant signing for shared cells extends existing infrastructure.

Shared hosting has the worst reputation in infrastructure — earned over twenty years of LAMP boxes where one tenant's bad day became everyone's. Why shared hosting got its bad name

Classic cPanel shared hosting ran arbitrary tenant code — PHP with filesystem access — on a cooperative-scheduled stack. A Barkpark shared cell is a different animal: tenants author content, not code. The workload is structured writes and cacheable reads against one well-understood schema. That single fact deletes the worst caveat outright — but not all of them. Here is the honest ledger.

What the architecture gives us for free

Zero tenant code
Tenants author content, not programs. The attack surface is our code, audited once — not a thousand strangers' plugins. This is the difference between shared Notion and shared cPanel.
BEAM preemption
Erlang was built for multi-tenant telecom: reductions-based preemptive scheduling, per-process heaps, millions of cheap processes. A runaway request cannot starve a neighbor's scheduler.
Workspace mobility
The tenant boundary is one atomic, walkable unit (workspace → projects → datasets → memberships). cPanel accounts were tar; workspaces are cargo.
Cacheable by nature
CMS spike traffic is public reads. Edge cache + webhook-driven purge absorbs 100× bursts without the cell noticing — elasticity for the price of a config block.
Fail-closed contract
Tenancy scoping already rescues to strict (multi_tenant? → true on error) and teardown is lifecycle-safe (delete_workspace walks media + docs + hooks).

The dwb-10 warm pool + reconciler already scales the fleet; new cells come up pre-baked in ≤15s when existing cells fill.

The doctrine — best of all worlds

• Cells, not silos. Capped at ~100 workspaces on a cax31, region-pinned, blue/green-deployed, canaried. Blast radius is a design number, not an accident.
• Two walls, one truth. App-layer scoping stays canonical; Postgres RLS becomes the second wall. A leak now requires the same bug twice, in different layers.
• Transparent limits. Meters visible in Studio and bp usage; soft limits with grace windows; a full quota reads as an invitation to grow, never a silent failure.
• Graduation, not punishment. The hot tenant gets a one-command live migrate to dedicated — same domain, same token, zero read downtime. The shared tier's ceiling is the dedicated tier's front door.
• Shared-cell profile. A hardened boot profile for cells: tmux console OFF, instance-admin surfaces fenced to the operator, webhooks egress-filtered, media processing in a sandboxed queue.
• Abuse isolation in minutes. Freeze the workspace (suspend), migrate neighbors nothing — reputation lives in the central mail relay, so a bad actor never taints an IP the cell depends on.

Barkpark · Cloud · shared-tier doctrine

Shared Cells — shared hosting without the sins

every caveat on the table · classic sins vs BEAM reality · the best-of-all-worlds doctrine

Shared hosting has the worst reputation in infrastructure — earned over twenty years of LAMP boxes where one tenant's bad day became everyone's. Barkpark's shared tier only deserves to exist if we can name every one of those sins, show which ones this architecture structurally cannot commit, and write doctrine for the rest. This paper is that ledger, and the synthesis: cells, not silos — with a graduation path instead of a ceiling.

~€0.12/mo
infra cost per tenant (100/cell)
1 row insert
provisioning a tenant
0
lines of tenant code executed
5
consumers of per-workspace export

Shared hosting earned its bad name from a sin Barkpark cannot commit: executing strangers' code on the same box.

Why shared hosting got its bad name

Classic cPanel shared hosting ran arbitrary tenant code — PHP with filesystem access — on a cooperative-scheduled stack. Every sin follows from that: one infinite loop starved the box (no preemption), one compromised WordPress owned every neighbor (shared filesystem, shared user contexts), inode limits hid until you hit them, and accounts were so sticky that rebalancing meant a support ticket and a weekend. A Barkpark shared cell is a different animal: tenants author content, not code. The workload is structured writes and cacheable reads against one well-understood schema. That single fact deletes the worst caveat outright — but not all of them. Here is the honest ledger.

The caveat ledger — all ten, honestly

CaveatClassic shared hostingBarkpark shared cellDoctrine
1 · Noisy neighborOne PHP loop starves the box; no preemption.Weaker by construction: BEAM preempts by reductions — no tenant can hog a scheduler. Real risks are shared Postgres connections, disk, and vips media work.Per-workspace rate limits + PG connection budget + media queue with backpressure; pressure score per workspace; hot tenant → graduate, don't throttle-to-death.
2 · Security blast radiusTenant code execution → one hacked plugin owns the box.No tenant code runs, ever. bp sites is static-only. Residual risk is app bugs: scoping leaks, SSRF via webhooks, media-parser CVEs.Defense in depth: app scoping + Postgres RLS as second wall; egress-filtered webhooks; vips in a sandboxed queue worker; shared-cell profile fences every instance-admin surface (tmux console OFF).
3 · Data isolationShared MySQL, tenant-visible filesystems.One Postgres, workspace_id row scoping; multi_tenant?/0 fail-closed. A scoping bug is still a cross-tenant leak.Add RLS policies keyed on a per-request app.workspace_id GUC — the same bug must now be made twice, in two layers, to leak.
4 · Fate sharingBox dies → hundreds down for hours; restore = ticket.Same physics — a cell outage hits every tenant on it.Cap cell size (~100 workspaces); blue/green per cell; archive/resurrect drills; per-workspace restore so one tenant's recovery never waits on the cell's.
5 · IP & mail reputationOne spammer blacklists the shared IP for everyone.Identical risk if cells send mail directly.Shared cells never send directly — all mail through the central DKIM relay with per-tenant signing + outbound rate caps; abuse freezes the workspace, not the cell.
6 · Performance ceilingHit the wall → buy a VPS → migrate by hand over a weekend.The cell is still finite.The ceiling becomes a door: live workspace migration to a dedicated box, domain intact (domains-table cutover). Graduation is an upsell moment, not an outage.
7 · Backup granularityAccount backups existed — restores were slow, lossy, ticket-driven.Instance-level archive/resurrect exists; per-workspace does not yet.Per-workspace export/bundle — the keystone primitive (see below). Self-serve restore from Studio.
8 · Upgrade couplingPHP upgrade breaks half the tenants at once.One BEAM per cell → all tenants upgrade together; a regression hits the whole cell.Canary cells first (the fleet already deploys blue/green); version pinning is a dedicated-tier feature, stated honestly, not promised on shared.
9 · Compliance & residency“Where is my data?” — no answer.A cell lives in exactly one region; per-tenant residency inside a shared cell is impossible.Region-pinned cells (EU default, Hetzner); residency choosers pick their cell at signup; strict-compliance customers are pointed at dedicated — honestly, at signup, not after.
10 · Hidden limitsInode caps and CPU-seconds discovered only at the wall; silent failure.Nothing hidden yet because no limits exist yet — the gap cuts both ways.Quotas are a visible product surface: live meters in Studio + bp usage, soft limits with grace windows, never a silent write failure. Transparency IS the differentiator.

Risk, scored

Same ten caveats, scored 1–9 (higher = worse). “With doctrine” assumes the build section below is shipped:

classic sharedBP cell todaywith doctrinenoisy neighborsecurity blast radiusdata isolationfate sharingmail reputationperf ceilingbackup granularityupgrade couplingresidencyhidden limits
less more

What the architecture gives us for free

Zero tenant code
Tenants author content, not programs. The attack surface is our code, audited once — not a thousand strangers' plugins. This is the difference between shared Notion and shared cPanel.
BEAM preemption
Erlang was built for multi-tenant telecom: reductions-based preemptive scheduling, per-process heaps, millions of cheap processes. A runaway request cannot starve a neighbor's scheduler.
Workspace mobility
The tenant boundary is one atomic, walkable unit (workspace → projects → datasets → memberships). cPanel accounts were tar; workspaces are cargo.
Cacheable by nature
CMS spike traffic is public reads. Edge cache + webhook-driven purge absorbs 100× bursts without the cell noticing — elasticity for the price of a config block.
Fail-closed contract
Tenancy scoping already rescues to strict (multi_tenant? → true on error) and teardown is lifecycle-safe (delete_workspace walks media + docs + hooks).
Warm capacity
The dwb-10 warm pool + reconciler already scales the fleet; new cells come up pre-baked in ≤15s when existing cells fill.

The doctrine — best of all worlds

  • Cells, not silos. Capped at ~100 workspaces on a cax31, region-pinned, blue/green-deployed, canaried. Blast radius is a design number, not an accident.
  • Two walls, one truth. App-layer scoping stays canonical; Postgres RLS becomes the second wall. A leak now requires the same bug twice, in different layers.
  • Transparent limits. Meters visible in Studio and bp usage; soft limits with grace windows; a full quota reads as an invitation to grow, never a silent failure.
  • Graduation, not punishment. The hot tenant gets a one-command live migrate to dedicated — same domain, same token, zero read downtime. The shared tier's ceiling is the dedicated tier's front door.
  • Shared-cell profile. A hardened boot profile for cells: tmux console OFF, instance-admin surfaces fenced to the operator, webhooks egress-filtered, media processing in a sandboxed queue.
  • Abuse isolation in minutes. Freeze the workspace (suspend), migrate neighbors nothing — reputation lives in the central mail relay, so a bad actor never taints an IP the cell depends on.
